object.medium: Pen and ink in a leather-bound pocket notebook
object.description: 'I think', and then a spindly branching diagram: a page from the pocket notebook Darwin opened in July 1837, nine months after the Beagle brought him home. He was twenty-eight and writing only for himself. The '1' at the base is a common ancestor; the branches ending in cross-bars are living species, the bare ones have died out. Underneath he reasons it through: if one ancestor is to give rise to as many living forms as exist now, and to groups of similar species, then extinction must be part of the process, and the gaps between living genera, 'A and B', 'C and B', record how long ago their lines parted. It is the first drawing of the tree of life as a genealogy rather than a ladder of perfection, and it came twenty-two years before On the Origin of Species, whose single illustration is a tidied version of this sketch. Darwin kept the notebooks all his life; this one is now in Cambridge University Library. It is in Notebook B, the tree of life.
facts: Notebook B is the first of a series Darwin lettered B to E on the 'transmutation of species', kept from 1837 to 1839.
Darwin did not read Malthus, whose essay on population gave him the mechanism of natural selection, until September 1838, after this sketch.
The notebook measures about the size of a hand and travelled in Darwin's pocket; some pages were later cut out and reused.
The one figure in On the Origin of Species (1859) is a branching diagram descended from this page.
